claims.text: Business activity is the process of combining resources - natural, human and man-made - to produce goods or services that satisfy the wants and needs of customers.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The purpose of business activity is to satisfy wants and needs by turning resources into output customers value more highly than the money they give up for it; because people specialise in one occupation and buy the rest of what they consume, a business can sell far more of one product than any single household could use.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Businesses do not share one purpose: privately owned firms usually pursue profit for their owners, state-owned and public-sector organisations pursue a service objective set by government, and social enterprises pursue a social or environmental aim while still needing to cover their costs.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Revenue from customers is what pays for the resources a business uses, so a business producing something customers do not want, or cannot afford at the price charged, tends to exhaust its money and stop trading.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Land, as a factor of production, means the natural resources a business uses: the site it occupies and the water, minerals, timber, grazing, fish stocks and climate it draws on.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Labour, as a factor of production, means the human effort, physical and mental, that people supply in producing goods and services.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Capital, as a factor of production, means the man-made resources used to produce other goods and services: machinery, vehicles, buildings, tools and equipment. In this sense capital is equipment rather than money; money is what a business uses to buy capital.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Enterprise, as a factor of production, means the willingness and ability to bring land, labour and capital together, decide what to produce and how, and carry the risk that the venture makes a loss.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Production needs all four factors together - a site, equipment and workers with nobody willing to organise them and bear the risk produce nothing - but the proportions differ by activity: a Namibian cattle farm is land-intensive, a call centre labour-intensive, and a zinc refinery capital-intensive.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Added value is the difference between the price a business charges for its output and the cost of the bought-in materials, components and services used to produce it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Added value per unit = selling price per unit - cost of bought-in materials and components per unit. For a period, total added value = sales revenue - cost of bought-in goods and services.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Added value is not profit. Wages, rent, power, marketing, insurance and interest are paid out of added value, and profit is what remains after all of them.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business can raise added value by raising the price customers are willing to pay - through branding, quality, design, convenience or service - or by lowering the cost of what it buys in. Raising price works where customers see a difference worth paying for; where they do not, higher prices tend to cost sales volume, and total added value can fall even though added value per unit has risen.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Economic activity is the use of scarce resources to produce goods and services. Resources are scarce in the sense that there are not enough of them to satisfy every want, so any use of a resource rules out another use and choice cannot be avoided by consumers, businesses or governments.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Opportunity cost is the benefit of the next best alternative given up when a choice is made.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Opportunity cost is identified by naming the single next best alternative forgone. It is not the sum of every alternative, and it is not the money spent - a business that spends N$400 000 on a delivery vehicle has an opportunity cost of whatever the best other use of that N$400 000 would have returned.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Ignoring opportunity cost leads a business to accept any option showing a positive return, when the resource it uses might have earned more in its next best use; the decision then raises profit less than an alternative would have done, and the shortfall does not appear anywhere in the accounts.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The business environment is dynamic, meaning that the conditions a business trades in change over time rather than staying fixed.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The sources of change a business faces are customer tastes and incomes, technology, the actions of competitors, laws and regulations, economic conditions such as interest rates, inflation and exchange rates, social attitudes, and the natural environment.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A change in the environment reaches a business through its revenue or its costs, and the size of the effect depends on how much of that business's sales or spending is exposed to the thing that changed; a business that monitors the change and adjusts what it offers tends to keep more of its customers than one that does not.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The Namibian dollar is pegged one-for-one with the South African rand, so Namibian businesses buying from South Africa are not exposed to a rate movement between the two currencies, while a fall of the rand against other currencies raises the Namibian dollar price of goods bought from outside the Common Monetary Area.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Businesses that succeed tend to have a product customers want at a price they will pay, enough cash to meet obligations as they fall due, managers with relevant experience, costs low enough to leave a margin, and the willingness to change what they offer as the market changes.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The common causes of business failure are running out of cash, a weak or mis-researched market, inexperienced management, uncontrolled costs, expanding faster than the business can finance, and an external shock such as the loss of a major customer or a sharp fall in demand.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business can be profitable and still fail. Profit is recorded when a sale is made, but if customers pay sixty days later while wages and suppliers must be paid now, the business can run out of cash, lose supply on credit, and be unable to continue trading.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Failure usually has several causes acting together rather than one, which is why a single remedy - more finance, or a price cut - often does not save a failing business on its own.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: New businesses fail more often than established ones because they have no trading record to raise finance against, no established customers to carry a bad month, and owners learning the market while spending money in it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A local business sells to customers in one town, settlement or district and usually operates from a single site.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A national business sells across the whole of one country, usually from several sites or through national distribution.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An international business is based in one country and sells to customers in other countries, typically by exporting.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A multinational business owns or controls production or service operations in more than one country, rather than only selling into them.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Local, national, international and multinational businesses are separated by the same dimensions: how far their customers are spread, whether they produce in more than one country, how much finance and management the operation needs, and how much exposure they carry to exchange rates, foreign law and foreign competition.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Moving from exporting to producing abroad raises both the potential market and the demands on the business: more finance, more managers, more than one legal and tax system to comply with, and exchange-rate exposure on costs as well as on revenue.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An entrepreneur is a person who sets up and runs a business, supplying the enterprise factor of production and bearing the financial risk of whether it succeeds.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An intrapreneur is an employee who develops new products, processes or ventures inside an existing business, using the employer's resources, with the employer carrying the financial risk.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The qualities associated with success in both roles include spotting an opportunity others have missed, creativity, willingness to take calculated risks, determination through setbacks, self-confidence, organisation, and the ability to persuade other people.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The two roles need the same qualities pointed at different obstacles. An entrepreneur has to persuade customers, suppliers and providers of finance outside the business, and stands to lose personal savings if it fails. An intrapreneur has to persuade managers inside the business to release budget and time, and risks reputation and promotion rather than personal savings.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Risk-taking is a business quality where it is calculated rather than blind: committing money without researching whether customers want the product is gambling, and what distinguishes successful entrepreneurs is judgement about which risks are worth taking.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Entrepreneurship is what turns an idea into a trading business: the entrepreneur identifies an unmet want, decides what to produce and how, assembles land, labour and capital, provides or raises the finance, and takes responsibility for the outcome. After suppliers, employees and lenders have been paid, the entrepreneur takes what is left, which may be a profit, nothing, or a loss.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The usual route from idea to trading business runs: identify the opportunity, research the market, write a business plan, raise the finance, choose and register a legal form, obtain premises, equipment and staff, and begin trading.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Because a start-up has no trading record, the entrepreneur's own savings, family money and personal reputation often carry the business until sales are established, and providers of external finance may ask for security or evidence of demand before committing.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Entrepreneurship raises output that would otherwise not exist: the resources a new business employs - a vacant plot, an unemployed school-leaver, an idle vehicle - produce nothing until somebody combines them, which is why the enterprise factor is described as organising the other three.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Intrapreneurship contributes to the ongoing success of an established business by producing new products, services and working methods from employees who already understand its customers, its operations and its constraints, and it helps to retain ambitious employees who might otherwise leave to start their own business.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business selling the same products year after year is exposed when tastes or technology move, so innovation generated inside the business reduces the risk of being overtaken by a competitor that moves first.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Developing an idea inside an established business spreads its cost across an operation that already has customers, premises and cash flow, so a failed experiment is absorbed rather than fatal - which is the difference between an intrapreneur's failed project and an entrepreneur's failed business.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Intrapreneurship happens where management provides time, a budget and tolerance of experiments that do not work; where every failure is punished, employees tend to stop proposing anything untried, and the business keeps the appearance of innovation without the substance.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The main barriers to entrepreneurship are lack of finance and of security to offer against it, lack of business skills and experience, lack of a researched idea, fear of failure, the time and cost of meeting registration, licensing and tax requirements, competition from established businesses, and weak infrastructure such as unreliable power, transport or internet.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Finance is a barrier because a new business has no trading record: a provider of finance judges repayment on evidence, and with little evidence it may decline, may offer less than the amount needed, or may ask for security the entrepreneur does not have.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Established competitors are a barrier because their larger scale gives them a lower cost per unit, recognised brands and existing supply agreements, so a new entrant may have to accept a thinner margin or find a segment the incumbents serve poorly.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The opportunity cost of starting a business is itself a barrier: leaving paid employment means giving up a known income for an uncertain one, which weighs most heavily on a person supporting a household.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Barriers can be lowered rather than removed - through training and mentoring, government or development-bank finance schemes aimed at start-ups, simplified registration, and incubators that share premises and advice - and which barrier binds hardest differs from one entrepreneur to the next.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Risk, in business, is a possible outcome whose likelihood can be estimated from experience or data, so it can be planned for, insured against or reduced.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Uncertainty is a possible future event whose likelihood cannot meaningfully be estimated, because there is no comparable experience to judge it from.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Risk and uncertainty are separated by whether a likelihood can be attached. A bakery whose records show that about 6% of loaves go unsold each day faces a risk it can price for; the chance that a new disease closes the border next year is an uncertainty, and no percentage can honestly be put on it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Business risk is the variability of a business's returns caused by the ordinary conditions of trading - demand, competition, costs and operations - and it falls on the owners, because they are paid after suppliers, employees and lenders.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Businesses handle risk by reducing it through research, maintenance and quality control, transferring it through insurance and fixed-price contracts, spreading it across several products or markets, and holding cash reserves. Uncertainty cannot be estimated, so it is handled by keeping flexibility and reserves rather than by calculation.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Business enterprise contributes to a country's development by creating jobs and incomes, raising output, generating tax revenue, using local resources, earning or saving foreign currency, and building skills in the workforce.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Employment created by new businesses raises household incomes, and the spending of those incomes in local shops and services supports further businesses and further jobs, so the initial effect is multiplied through the local economy.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Enterprise widens the tax base - profitable businesses pay tax and their employees pay tax on earnings - which funds the schools, clinics and roads a developing economy needs; and a business that processes a local raw material instead of exporting it unprocessed keeps more of the added value inside the country.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The development effect depends on conditions: it is larger where the businesses survive and grow, where they employ and train local people rather than importing staff, where profits are reinvested in the country rather than removed from it, and where the activity does not exhaust the resources other livelihoods depend on.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business plan is a written document setting out what a business intends to do, how it intends to do it, who will do it, and what financial results it expects, usually covering the first one to three years.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business plan serves two audiences. Inside the business it forces the owner to think the idea through and provides targets to manage against; outside it gives providers of finance the evidence they need to judge the proposal.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Writing the plan reduces risk because the research it requires can expose a fatal flaw - no market at the price assumed, a cost not allowed for, a month when cash runs out - while that flaw still costs only the time spent finding it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A plan is also a control document: once trading begins, actual sales, costs and cash are compared with the forecasts in it, and a gap between the two is a signal to investigate rather than a verdict on its own.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business plan normally contains an executive summary; a description of the business, its ownership and objectives; the product or service and what distinguishes it; market research on customers, market size and competitors; a marketing plan; an operations plan covering premises, equipment, suppliers and staffing; the management team and their experience; financial forecasts; the finance required and what it will be used for; and the main risks with the steps planned to handle them.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The financial forecasts in a plan normally include start-up costs, a forecast of revenue and costs, a cash-flow forecast month by month, and a break-even calculation.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The market research section carries the weight of the plan because the sales forecast rests on it, and the sales forecast drives the revenue figure, the cash-flow forecast and the amount of finance requested; a sales figure with nothing behind it makes every later number unsupported too.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The executive summary is written last and read first: in about a page it states what the business is, what it needs and what it expects, so that a reader can decide whether to read further.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The benefits of a business plan are that it forces research before money is committed, strengthens the case put to providers of finance, sets targets for monitoring, and coordinates the people involved around one set of objectives.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A plan improves the chance of raising finance because a provider of finance is assessing whether the business can repay: a plan showing researched demand, costed operations and a month-by-month cash-flow forecast gives them evidence on which to judge, and its absence leaves them judging on very little.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The limitations of a business plan are that its forecasts rest on assumptions that may be wrong, that it dates quickly in a changing environment, that preparing it takes time and money a small start-up may not have, and that a well-written plan can create confidence the underlying business has not earned.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A plan written mainly to obtain finance tends to carry optimistic figures, and those figures then make a poor benchmark for managing the business, so the same document can satisfy the provider of finance and mislead the owner.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Whether a full written plan is worth the effort depends on what it is for. Where external finance is sought, a plan is usually required and the effort is unavoidable. Where the business is small, self-financed and able to change direction quickly, a short plan kept current may be more useful than a long one that goes out of date and is never revisited.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
